title: Artificial Neurons and the Perceptron
oneLiner: An artificial neuron adds up weighted inputs and fires if the total is big enough; the perceptron learns those weights from its mistakes.

what.html:
An artificial neuron is a tiny calculator inspired by brain cells. It multiplies each input by a weight (how important that input is), adds them up with a bias, and passes the total through an activation function to produce its output.

Everyday versionDeciding whether to go for a run: sunshine counts +2, being tired counts −3, a friend joining counts +2. Add them up; if the total clears your threshold, you go. Adjust how much each factor counts after the runs you regretted: that is learning.

The perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958) is the simplest such neuron: it outputs one class if the weighted sum is ≥ 0, the other otherwise, and it has a simple rule for learning its weights.

why.html:
• The building block of every neural network: deep networks are just many neurons connected in layers.
  • Learning = adjusting weights. The knowledge of a network is stored in its connection weights.
  • It shows the limits that motivated deep learning: a single perceptron can't solve XOR, which is why we need hidden layers.

how.title: The biological inspiration
how.html: The brain has about 1010 neurons, each with 104–105 connections. Neurons switch slowly (about a millisecond), yet you recognise a scene in a second: only ~100 sequential steps, so the brain must compute massively in parallel. A neuron's dendrites receive signals, the cell body processes them, the axon sends the output, and synapses connect neurons.

how.title: The artificial neuron
how.html: Inputs x₁…xₙ, weights w₁…wₙ, bias b: compute z = Σ wᵢxᵢ + b, then ŷ = f(z). Each weight says how important its feature is; the bias shifts the threshold. The neuron outputs one number.

how.title: Biological vs artificial
how.html: Real neurons use complex biochemistry, analogue signals and adaptive synapses, are fault-tolerant and learn by experience. Artificial neurons are simple maths: digital, with adjustable weights, learning by algorithms, deterministic. They keep only the essential computational idea.

how.title: Networks of neurons
how.html: Connect many neurons in layers (input, hidden, output) and you get an artificial neural network. Connections can be feed-forward, recurrent or self-loops. Networks are highly parallel, tune their weights automatically, and can approximate complex functions. Use them when inputs are high-dimensional (raw sensor data), data are noisy, the target function is unknown and explainability isn't critical: speech, images, financial prediction.

how.title: Connectionism
how.html: The idea behind neural networks: intelligence emerges from many simple units; all knowledge lives in the connections; learning changes connection strengths; processing is parallel and distributed.

how.title: The perceptron's rule
how.html: ŷ = 1 if Σ wᵢxᵢ + b ≥ 0, otherwise −1 (classical) or 0 (the convention used in the worked examples). Both conventions work; only the threshold calculation changes.

how.title: Logic gates with one neuron
how.html: With x₀ = 1 for the bias: AND works with w₀ = −1, w₁ = w₂ = 0.75 (only 1 + 1 clears the threshold); OR with w₀ = −1, w₁ = w₂ = 2 (any single 1 clears it). Geometrically, each is a straight line separating the "1" corners from the "0" corners.

how.title: How the perceptron learns
how.html: Go through the examples. If the prediction is right, do nothing. If it's wrong, nudge every weight: wᵢ ← wᵢ + η(t − ŷ)xᵢ. Too low an output raises the weights of active inputs; too high lowers them. Repeat until a full pass makes no mistakes. If the data are linearly separable, this is guaranteed to happen in a finite number of steps.

how.title: A learning trace: the NOT gate
how.html: Start at w₀ = w₁ = 0, η = 1. Epoch 1: input 1 is wrongly classified, so the weights become (−1, −1). Epoch 2: input 0 is now wrong, so w₀ goes back to 0. Epoch 3: both right: done, with w₁ = −1, w₀ = 0.

how.title: The XOR problem
how.html: XOR is 1 when exactly one input is 1. Put the four points on a square: the 1s are on one diagonal, the 0s on the other. No straight line separates them, so no single perceptron can compute XOR. The fix is multiple layers with non-linear activations (the multilayer perceptron).

how.title: Linearly separable data
how.html: Two classes are linearly separable in n dimensions if an (n − 1)-dimensional hyperplane separates them (a line in 2-D, a plane in 3-D). Then infinitely many separating lines exist and the perceptron will find one. Writing x̃ = (1, x₁, …, xₙ) and w = (w₀, …, wₙ), the perceptron is just ŷ = step(wᵀx̃).

demo.html: Press Next example to replay the NOT-gate trace step by step: it converges in epoch 3 with w = [0, −1]. Switch to AND or OR and run to convergence. Then choose XOR: the weights keep changing epoch after epoch and never settle.

example.html:
Logic gates: AND, OR and NOT are each a single perceptron; XOR needs two layers (e.g. XOR = (x₁ OR x₂) AND NOT(x₁ AND x₂)).

Where networks shine: speech recognition, image classification, financial prediction: high-dimensional, noisy inputs with an unknown target function.

Supplementary A single-neuron alarm on a base station: z = 2·(drop-rate above 2%) + 1.5·(RSRP below −110 dBm) − 2.5; raise a ticket if z ≥ 0. A perceptron can learn such weights from past tickets.

misunderstandings: A perceptron can learn any rule given enough time.
Only linearly separable rules; for XOR it never converges.
Without it the boundary must pass through the origin; NOT and AND need it.
Artificial neurons work like real neurons.
They are drastically simplified abstractions of one computational idea.
Using {0, 1} vs {−1, +1} outputs changes what a perceptron can do.
Both are equivalent; only the threshold/bias arithmetic differs.
takeaways: An artificial neuron computes z = Σwᵢxᵢ + b and outputs ŷ = f(z); weights store knowledge.
The perceptron uses a step/sign activation: a linear classifier.
AND, OR, NOT are linearly separable and each needs one perceptron (e.g. AND: −1, 0.75, 0.75; OR: −1, 2, 2).
Learning rule: wᵢ ← wᵢ + η(t − ŷ)xᵢ, repeated until no mistakes; converges for linearly separable data.
XOR is not linearly separable: a single perceptron fails, so we need multi-layer networks.
thirty: An artificial neuron, inspired by biological neurons, multiplies each input by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the sum through an activation function. The perceptron is the simplest case: it outputs 1 if the weighted sum is at least zero and 0 (or −1) otherwise, so it draws a straight line between two classes. It learns by going through examples and, whenever it is wrong, changing each weight by the learning rate times the error times the input. If the data can be separated by a line this always converges, which is enough for AND, OR and NOT. XOR cannot be separated by any line, which is why we need multi-layer networks.
